newsitem.title: INDIA: India moves to cut bulging sugar stocks.
newsitem.headline: India moves to cut bulging sugar stocks.

text.p: India's decision to end a trading agency's monopoly over sugar exports will spur domestic competition and cut bulging stocks, industry officials and analysts said on Monday.
But the move is no quick fix for the sugar industry which over the longer term will have trouble competing on the world market unless productivity is increased, analysts said.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet decided last week to end the export monopoly of the Indian Sugar and General Industries Export Import Corp (ISIGEC), a private company set up by the sugar milling industry.
"It is good," said Ashok Gulati of the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER). "Earlier there was a cartel. The idea is to break that cartel."
Any firms registered with Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) can now export sugar, a government official said.
Sugar stocks have surged as production, spurred by eight consecutive plentiful monsoons, outstripped demand.

Output in the 1995/96 season which ends on September 30 is expected to reach 16.45 million tonnes, up sharply from 14.6 million in the previous crop year. Yearly consumption is about about 13 million tonnes.
India's sugar surplus is expected to swell to 8.0 million tonnes by October 1, up from 5.4 million one year earlier at the start of the 1995/96 season, industry officials said.
Analysts said an increase in the number of exporters would help sell at least some of the surplus to foreign buyers.
The government decision on exports was considered an important step towards freeing the sugar industry from a decades-old system of licensing, pricing and distribution.

India began abolishing licences for many industries under an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991, But it kept sugar under the old regime which has subsidised the price for consumers and protected producers.
After Deve Gowda took office in June, his centre-left United Front minority coalition vowed to do away with a licensing system which has kept government control over sugar production.
The decision to allow more firms to export was seen as a step towards more sweeping liberalisation.
The sugar industry slammed the government's decision.
"For the short term it is very bad and in the long term it is not good at all," said S.L. Jain, secretary general of the Indian Sugar Mills Association.
Jain predicted the quality of exports would suffer and export earnings would plummet, hurting India's trade balance.
He said the sugar industry expected to lose some 350 million rupees ($9.8 million) on sugar exports in 1996/97 due to declining international sugar prices.
The loss could rise to 500 million rupees ($14 million) following the decision to allow more exporters, he said.
Civil Supplies Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told parliament on Monday the decision would spur manufacturers to produce quality sugar and export directly.

Gulati said the decision was a way to cut stocks, but more steps would be needed to make producers competitive on the world market. He cited the need for better irrigation in the sugar belt in the western state of Maharashtra.
